rv.q: Even when Connor’s Romeo and Zegler’s Juliet square off from opposite sides of the venue, their invisible chains – hormones, by another term – are magic.

“Romeo + Juliet” is still telling the Bard’s old story with its old bones, but this production really is the fresh voice it markets itself to be. Gold’s specific convictions are vague, but the story he’s retelling remains captivating, fun and, eventually, even gutting.
It's high-energy theatre that envelops you from all directions.
It’s the least boring or cringe Shakespeare I’ve seen in a long time.
Gold's revival fully commits to its concept and sustains it surprisingly well... this R+J is an infectious emotional rollercoaster.
But this doesn’t detract from a lively, funny, charming production, or from its youthful vigour and talented cast.
Gold and his company seem most comfortable in these swoony sections. The fights are silly; the final scene in the tomb is bizarrely quick and awkward.
...Sam Gold’s frenzied, youthful staging of the Shakespeare tragedy.
The play is thus less terrifying than teenifying — hence the plus sign instead of the “and” in the title.

But those newcomers may be surprised to find that what they thought was a tragedy about young people crushed by societal constraints is actually the sad tale of two nice kids who die from a lack of adult supervision.
It is all, as one can probably imagine, a lot, at once disarming and confusing.
Alas, while the two leads are sincere, the show itself is (a) altogether too much of too much; (b) a bit of an ill-focused mess; and (c) less than engrossing.
Unfortunately, the production’s rave-like, nihilistic drive does little to make up for its lack of clarity or a pulse.
What we have here instead is a fun night out and a hangover.
But, without question, Kit Connor’s Romeo is the sole reason to get thee to the theater.

One could be forgiven for walking away from this show’s two (and a half) hours’ traffic thinking that maybe Romeo and Juliet is kind of mid after all. Such is the enervating effect of so aggressively clickbaity and uncurious a production.
A new production, one like you’ve likely never seen, with standout performances and a fabulous and aligned design team, Romeo + Juliet defies the stars and brings magic to Circle in the Square.
Sam Gold has made it an exciting and thoroughly engaging experience for audiences of all ages.
In every aspect, Connor delivers one of the most impressive Broadway debuts in many years.
It's all a very pleasant surprise that this Romeo + Juliet is more akin to Skins than expected: wildly enjoyable, acutely contemporary, potently acted.
...this production is more for the kids
Those theatergoers unencumbered by memories of other productions of Romeo and Juliet may more easily embrace this post-modern take on Shakespeare's tragedy.
The kids aren’t all right, and if their story is not really a full-blown tragedy anymore, they’re awfully fun to watch.
The stellar production succeeds in threading the needle between two nearly impossible tasks that come with putting on Romeo + Juliet.
The cast’s relative lack of stage experience is manifest in a flattening of both the poetry and the tragedy.
But for slightly older audiences, now nursing heartburn more often than heartbreak, you’ll probably just feel exhausted.
With its energetic and game cast, Romeo + Juliet on Broadway is enjoyable, but uneven.
While Connor and Zegler are passionate as Romeo and Juliet, they display little chemistry when together.
But double- and even triple-casting has its pitfalls.
Her speech before taking the sleeping potion, for instance, sounds more like rhetorical fancies than a child’s frightened thoughts about what could go wrong.
The entire production flagrantly panders to them, so perhaps they’ll appreciate it more than older folks.
Somehow, it’s sad to be confronted with the news that the violence so stealthily and widely afflicting our society today has infiltrated so far as to include treating Shakespeare’s text violently.
It makes Shakespeare accessible, relatable, and enjoyable.
Simultaneously relevant and faithful to the source material, this adaptation is more than its tagline, “the youth are fucked.”

Gold’s adaptation feels like a high school senior’s dissertation of the play that focuses on odd moments (the nurse’s monologue about her child) and totally disregards bigger moments (like the fight with Paris at the end of the play) to fix his thesis.
What’s more problematic is that Gold doesn’t appear to have any unifying approach to the play aside from creating moments that might play well on TikTok or Instagram Reels.

cn.t: Sam Gold's Gen Z-targeted revival divides critics with its aggressively modern, club-like aesthetic. Connor and Zegler earn praise, but reactions split on whether the hyperactive, pop-infused production enhances or overshadows Shakespeare's tragedy.

vs.sum: Broadway's only thrust-stage theater offers an unmatched intimate experience — no seat is more than a few rows from the action. Sightlines are excellent from every angle, though some seats face actors' backs during certain scenes.

acc.note: Elevator accessible through adjoining building. Loop technology and neck induction systems available.

vr.q: This new production of Romeo and Juliet on Broadway, starring Kit Connor and Rachel Zegler, is worth every bit of hype you're hearing about it.
